comparator.name: Biomedical Sciences
comparator.sourceNotes: The official prospective curriculum specifies 60 EC in each year. Years 1 and 2 contain integrated mechanisms, context/innovation, professionalism, patient contact and research lines; year 2 has 4.5 EC of free space. Year 3 specifies two 11-EC disciplinary minors, 3 EC of open elective space, 28 EC of bachelor research internship and 1 EC of writing alongside integrity, professionalism and patient contact. The year-three narrative calls the internship 27 EC, while its credit-bearing table lists 28 EC and totals 60 EC; the 28-EC table value is used. The minors are preserved as choices rather than assigned invented topics.

core: Molecular, cellular and physiological mechanisms of human health and disease
Laboratory, clinical and population investigation of disease and prevention
Quantitative methods, evidence appraisal and biomedical research ethics
Patient-oriented research and evidence-based healthcare innovation

Toxicology and chemical effects on health
questions: How do molecular and physiological processes produce illness and responses to treatment?
How do neural processes, perception and development relate to behaviour and mental health?
Which research evidence can improve patient care and prevention?

alternatives.label: Closest match to biomedical sciences
alternatives.concept: A biomedical programme integrating molecular and cellular mechanisms, human physiology, disease, laboratory investigation, epidemiology and quantitative evidence for understanding health and treatment. It retains research and patient-facing perspectives while lacking Radboud's required extended internship and innovation projects.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum centres on human biomedical mechanisms and methods, with population, clinical and behavioural study; the broad field label describes the whole programme.
progression: Foundations in life and health, data, mathematics and brain science precede molecular, laboratory, physiological, biomedical and advanced statistics courses. All formal prerequisites precede their dependants and every course is offered in its assigned semester.

alternatives.label: Neuroscience, cognition & health
alternatives.concept: A brain and health programme connecting neurobiology, sensory processing, cognition, language, development and mental health with human physiology, disease mechanisms, research synthesis and philosophy of mind.
alternatives.labelReason: The course sequence gives sustained weight to neural and cognitive processes, mental health and human biology, so the combined label reflects the actual curriculum.
alternatives.distinctness: Relative to the broad biomedical route, this programme replaces seven courses in epidemiology, laboratory methods, immunology, mathematical statistics and biomedical ethics with philosophy of mind and emotion, higher cognitive functions, psycholinguistics and abnormal psychology. These choices follow the evidenced neuroscience specialisation, not a numerical target.
progression: Brain and behaviour, life and health, data and philosophical foundations precede higher cognitive neuroscience, neurobiology, psychology and research synthesis. Formal prerequisites precede dependent courses and each course is offered in its assigned semester.

selection.assessment: The closest curriculum retains the molecular, physiological, clinical and population span; neuroscience supports a substantively different second route, with seven courses unique to each. Epidemiology, movement science, health technology assessment and toxicology are individually evidenced specialisations at Radboud, but the current UCR catalogue cannot sustain a distinct 24-course programme centred on any one without filling it with weakly related courses. We therefore stop at two.

blocks: Both introduce cellular and bodily mechanisms as a basis for studying health; Radboud integrates this with its first-quarter theme.
Both examine cellular processes and biological mechanisms; Radboud also integrates heredity and behaviour in this quarter.
Both study physiological regulation and the functioning of human organ systems.
Both examine disease processes including abnormal cell growth; Radboud's quarter also covers life stages.
Both investigate human structure and movement; Radboud integrates circulation and neural systems as well.
Both examine infection and immune defence; UCR concentrates these subjects in one advanced course.
Both explain disease mechanisms across organ systems; UCR does not mirror Radboud's personalised-healthcare sequence.
Radboud requires a scientific research project. UCR's advanced cognitive-science course develops experiment design but does not reproduce the required project.
Both introduce systematic research and statistical analysis in the study of human phenomena; the UCR course emphasises experiments.
Both develop empirical research practice, with UCR concentrating on molecular and biochemical laboratory work.
Both develop analysis of research observations; UCR offers a general data-science foundation rather than a biomedical-specific research line.
Both include quantitative analysis of evidence and large datasets; UCR teaches general predictive modelling.
Both require critical synthesis of healthcare-related research evidence; UCR's seminar emphasises systematic reviews and meta-analysis.
Radboud's context, science and innovation line integrates scientific work with innovation; UCR Ethics is narrower and is not presented as its direct counterpart.
Both study how evidence and stakeholder circumstances affect healthcare interventions; UCR concentrates on health psychology.

notes.text: Radboud integrates laboratory, clinical and population research throughout its biomedical programme and requires a 28-EC research internship plus innovation projects and two specialist minors. UCR offers substantial related biology, health and research methods, but these schedules do not reproduce that continuous specialist training or required internship.
